subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is for me, sir, a very real pleasure to extend to you my heartiest congratulations on your election to be the Speaker of this house. I join with my leader, as well as with others in this group and, indeed, with all groups in this chamber, in extending good wishes to those other hon. members who must, by now, know that we all offer them warmest congratulations.
Mr. Speaker, in the course of the last two or three speeches which I had the privilege of making in the recent campaign, I made an assertion which I feel sure could not be denied, and I made a prediction which I believe may well come true. My assertion was that the last parliament was just about the worst one we ever had. My prediction was that this parliament, which we were electing on April 8, could be one of the best we have ever had. I believed that to be so at the time I made the prediction. I believe it now. As a matter of fact, I believe it even more today than I did yesterday, for I think what happened in this house last night will play a salutory part in bringing my prophecy to reality.
(Mr. Hays.)
When I made the prediction that this parliament could well be one of the best we have had in the history of this country I did so saying at the same time that I thought we would have another minority government. I tried, therefore, to deal with the question: why could I hope that a parliament with a minority government would be a good one whereas the parliament just over, which also had a minority government, was such an awful one? My own answer to that question was this. I believed that no matter what party might be called on to form the government in this parliament it would realize that it should at all costs avoid an election, and that in order to do this it would have to pay some attention to the views of all members in the house. I said, also, that I felt it would have to pay some attention to the views of those of us who represent the New Democratic party.
The government learned yesterday that that is true; that although we, in common with all members of the house, feel that the people of Canada want us to stay here and do the business of the country, on important and crucial issues we shall not shrink from doing what is clearly our duty. I am sure all of us in the house hope that after the experience of yesterday the government of the day will drop its arrogance and realize it has to pay some attention to the wishes of parliament as a whole.
When I said that this parliament could be one of the best we have ever had, I had in mind not that this would just happen because someone predicted it or because a certain party formed the government, but rather because there were certain things which we, as members of this house, would have to do. If we want this to be a good parliament, and one which serves the people of Canada well, there are certain conscious efforts which we as members must make. I intend to speak of these conscious efforts under three main headings.
In the first place, I feel we in this parliament in all corners of this house must with determination practise strict adherence to the rights, privileges and procedures of parliament. I want to emphasize that this means something more than just literal adherence to the rules or standing orders set out in our book. It is easy enough to follow the simple rules which determine how long a member may speak, when the house shall sit, when it shall rise, and so on. Most of the written rules are easy enough to follow. But parliament consists not only of written rules of procedure but of certain rights, practices and traditions which have grown up over the years and over the centuries. If we are going to make this parliament work, if we are

going to make it the valuable democratic institution it could be, we have to pay regard to these rules, practices and traditions. In order to be specific as to some of the things in which I think this parliament must not fail, it will be necessary for me to refer to some of the failures of the past. I would make the plea that they not be repeated in this twenty sixth parliament.
Last year we had the experience of a full fiscal year passing without the people's representatives voting on the estimates of expenditure. A full fiscal year's money was spent, ten months of it on the basis of interim supply and the other two months on the basis of governor general's warrants. If my reading of Canadian history is correct, this is the first time this has happened. This sort of thing does damage to the institution of parliament. I call upon this government which has now taken over not to delay bringing down the estimates. Once they are down, I call upon the government not to delay in arranging for their discussion as early as possible in the fiscal year, so that they can be considered by hon. members of this house and can be passed before that money is almost entirely spent. The whole question of parliamentary control over the purse is one of the most important elements in parliamentary democracy, and it matters not how well we keep the written rules in the book if we fail to adhere to the principle of parliamentary control of the purse.
In the same vein I would mention the question of the budget. There are various definitions which one can give to a budget. Sometimes it is thought of merely as a series of taxation changes that the minister of finance brings before the house. It is that, but it is more than that: it is an accounting by the government to the people's representatives on the state of the nation's finances. It is almost two years since the House of Commons had a full debate on a budget dealing with the finances of this nation, and I urge this government to make sure that this error, this failure, is not repeated during the life of this parliament.
I remind the government also of the position in which it finds itself with regard to the surcharge order in council passed last June. The government now finds itself, according to an announcement made yesterday, in the position of feeling that it must introduce legislation validating an order in council which at one time the members of the government felt, as we felt, was completely invalid. It may be that the government of today has no alternative to the one suggested yesterday, but I am certainly very unhappy about
The Address-Mr. Knowles this proposed course because it seems to suggest that future governments who may feel they want to pass something by way of order in council which is of doubtful validity can say: "Oh well, a subsequent parliament will take care of it by legislation if there is any invalidity". Mr. Speaker, these are the kinds of things beyond the actual rules which are written in the books which are of great importance if we are going to maintain the rights and privileges and the importance of parliament.
Another of the errors of the last parliament, and another reason why it was such a poor one, was the great difficulty we had in getting to the floor of that parliament the tremendous issues which were of concern to the Canadian people at that time. I need not enumerate them now because we enumerated them during the course of the last session. We have already had that sort of trouble in this parliament, for it is only because we took advantage through the right of the leader of this group to move a subamendment yesterday that we had a discussion on the important issue of nuclear arms. But even though we had this discussion yesterday, it was virtually ex post facto because the government had already made an announcement which indicated a decision for the Canadian people had been made on this question.
Yesterday we were told by the Prime Minister that we should not be concerned about this; that after all there was an opportunity to vote confidence or non-confidence in the government, and that such action would show approval or disapproval of the government's decision. But I would remind the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), who is doing me the honour of paying attention to my remarks, that the Liberals in the last house did not agree that the votes of confidence which the government in the last session won gave validity to the surcharge order in council. True it is, in a constitutional sense, that if a government is maintained in power by votes of confidence the day to day things which it does have a kind of approval. But surely you do not stretch that constitutional theory to the point that it is giving approval of government decisions on major issues of policy.
The surcharge order issued last year was such a major issue. It involved the taxation of the Canadian people of hundreds of millions of dollars. It was enacted by order in council without reference to parliament at any point, and without the consent of the government of that day even to refer it to the supreme court. That was a wrong course to take. The nuclear arms issue is an issue of deep concern to all the people of Canada; it is perhaps the most significant issue facing the human race at the present time. I feel,.

The Address-Mr. Knowles as all members of our group feel, that it was improper and that it was a violation of the rights and traditions of parliamentary practice and procedure for the government to take a stand on this question before bringing it before this House of Commons. My plea to the government is to remember how its own members, when sitting on this side of the house last year, felt annoyed and affronted over the things done during that session, and I hope that they will not soon forget their annoyance but that they will realize that if parliament is to work they must pay attention to these niceties of the relationship between the executive and the parliament of Canada.
This is the most important aspect of responsible government. As I say, it depends not just on our being able to follow written rules which spell out some mechanical details; it depends on the government realizing all the time, day and night, week in week out, that it is responsible to parliament and that its proper relationship with parliament is something it must continually maintain.
In the same vein I feel that if parliament is to be seen as a place where democracy is being practised and where the people's representatives are speaking for them, a great deal of thought must go into the organization of the business of this house. I would pay tribute to the action of the Secretary of State for his holding already a meeting of representatives from all four parties, at which it was my privilege to represent this party. I understand he plans to hold other such meetings, and I welcome them and urge him not to let down on this. I urge the government to pay particular attention to the organization of the business of the house so that it will appear to the country that we are doing business, and so that the members of this house will feel this business is being done in an orderly manner.
Again I must mention some things which should not be done. I think it is a mistake to commence debate on a piece of legislation and then, because the government runs into some difficulty, to adjourn the debate and proceed with something else. I think it is a mistake to shuffle around from one piece of business to another. I think it is a mistake to keep the house guessing from day to day as to what is going to happen the next day or next week. I think it makes far more sense in terms of democracy and parliamentary practice for the government through this kind of four-party meeting which the Secretary of State has already held, to take the house into its confidence and to tell us what is being planned. Then once we commence a piece of

legislation we should stay with it until it is completed, and thus do our business in an orderly fashion.
A lot is said about the organization of the business of the house as though the main aim were to get it through and save time. We do not want to waste time, but that is not the main aim of parliamentary reform. The main aim is to make sure that our business is done efficiently and with expedition, and also to make sure that it is done with a sense of participation on the part of all members. I recognize that this is not a city council or a county council but the parliament of Canada. The government is the government, and it has certain responsibilities as the executive. It is also responsible to parliament. But the fact remains that the people in the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre are represented here not by the government but by their member. The people of Burnaby-Coquitlam are represented by their member, and those of other ridings by their members, and there are certain things in which the people of Canada are not really participating unless their members are taking part in these decisions. This is what was wrong with the spending of money last year. It was spent without the approval of the 265 members representing the 18 million people of Canada. It was spent as a result of decisions of the cabinet. I say, therefore, that the whole business of organizing the legislation, the discussions, the debates of this house is important, not just for the convenience of members. It is important that it appear that the whole of the parliament of Canada, all the representatives of the people of Canada, are taking part in the debates and in the legislation in this house.
I think also, Mr. Speaker, attention should be given to the whole question of how questions are answered. I realize, and I assert, that on the opposition side of the house we must not use the question period frivolously. Today's Hansard will show a number of questions which, in my view, should not have been asked. However, when serious questions are asked the government has the responsibility of giving answers as expeditiously as it can. I think we have far too many occasions upon which the answer is that government policy will be made known in due course, or that the question asked is one of which notice will be taken. We should forgive government members for a few days, perhaps, until ministers know their way around their departments. However, I think we should look upon the question period not as so much political warfare but as one of the most important parts of the political democracy we are practising in this country.

One of the things about the parliamentary-system that makes it superior to other legislative systems is precisely the fact that we are members representing our people in 265 constituencies and we are here on the floor of the House of Commons with the members of the government, in a position to ask them questions on behalf of the people we represent. This gives us the right to ask serious questions and to receive serious answers. The importance of asking serious questions and of receiving informative replies cannot be overemphasized.

I give this now, Mr. Speaker, as an example of the thing I think politicians, members of parliament, should avoid, this business of taking one position when you are on the government side of the house and taking another when you get to the opposition side, then changing again when you get back. It is not good for parliamentary democracy. It does not lead the public to have that kind of confidence in their representatives which the people of Canada want to have. I say the same thing to my friends of the Progressive

The Address-Mr. Knowles Conservative party. It is very interesting to hear some of them now asking from this side of the house for the government of the day to do the things that their government refused to do when they were over there.
Now, Mr. Speaker, is this really necessary? Must we have this kind of human weakness that results in a change in position as we move back and forth? If we persist in it, we cannot be surprised if there is cynicism in the public mind regarding politicians. I think it is unfortunate there is that cynicism. I think it is unfortunate that "politician" is sometimes thought of as a dirty word. I feel that a politician has a tremendously high calling, but it is up to us so to act in this house in our various parties that the people of Canada will come to that realization.
The third heading I have on this list of things I think we must do if we are going to make this parliament one of the best in our "history is that we must work to produce some solid legislation that will be of benefit to the Canadian people. In the first place, without delay, we must get on the statute books of this country legislation, and we must have brought before us government policies, that will get our economy rolling and keep it rolling. We must provide employment. I welcome the statement that was made by the hon. lady who moved the address. I welcome the statement made in this regard the other day by the Prime Minister. However, statements are not enough. We have to keep at this. Unemployment is not something that can be solved with one magic solution. It takes economic planning; it takes fiscal and financial policies that will stimulate the economy. It takes training. It takes all the various things our economists know must be done. This is the session of parliament in which we must do those things to provide employment and provide a thriving economy for our people.
The field of pensions is another in which we must produce a piece of solid legislation. I welcome the announcement in the speech from the throne that something is coming. I welcome the assurances that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss La-Marsh) has given me on a couple of occasions that if I will just contain myself these things will come to pass. But, Mr. Speaker, I insist that there must be no delay and that this legislation must be as good as or better than the Liberals are now proclaiming it to be. Though the indications so far are very good, in the sense that it looks like there will be an increase in the amount of the pension and that there will be a contributory plan and so on, I regret that there seems to be mo suggestion from the Liberal side of the

house that the means test is going to be removed at age 65. In my view this is one of those solid achievements that this session of this parliament ought to produce.
I regret too that in the speech from the throne there is no reference to health insurance or medicare. The year 1919 was the year when the Liberals first started talking in this field. It took them nearly 40 years to get hospitalization on the statute books. But, Mr. Speaker, medicare is one of the prime needs of the people of our time. There is a great deal of interest in it, as is being shown by the platforms of all parties in this country at the present time. This is a piece of legislation that must come out of this session.
Housing is another field in which we must make tremendous progress. Before my time runs out I should like to say that I think too, that in this session of this parliament we must make tremendous steps in the field of increasing our contribution to external aid. We in this corner of the house do not like the only decision that has been made so far in this parliament so far as international relations are concerned, namely, the decision that was taken last night. Over and above whatever defence or diplomatic arrangements have to be made, we think that if we are going to achieve and maintain peace in the world we have got to do something to raise the living standards of mankind the world around, and what we are doing in Canada is not even a drop in the bucket. When you look at that in the light of our unemployment and in the light of our unused capacity and unused resources, I suggest the time has come for the government to give to parliament and to the people of Canada a vision of what we can do as Canadians to help to improve the position of mankind throughout the world.
There are other fields, but I stress these five: the provision of full employment, including the whole question of the economy and economic planning; improvements in pensions, and I suggest that the least that should happen would be $75 a month at 65 right away, with the other things that the government has indicated; then, housing; also medicare, and finally a contribution to the peace of the world. I see you are on the edge of your chair, Mr. Speaker. I am through. I just want to emphasize my belief that the prediction I made before the election was held is one that we can make come true. We can make this parliament one of the best that the people of Canada have ever had. We can do it, if we will adhere strictly to the traditions and practices of parliament, if we will do our best to establish in the

public mind confidence in us as their representatives, and if we will work together to bring down some very solid legislation for the good of the people of Canada.

Now from the legislative program offered in the speech from the throne I would particularly like to dwell on the economic measures mainly meant to remedy unemployment.
I do not have to recall that the government intends to establish a department of industry, that it will add $100 million to the funds at the disposal of the Atlantic development board. The government intends to create a municipal development and loan board. It also intends to create a Canada development corporation and to establish an economic council of Canada.
When the bills are before us we will, I am sure, be able to see exactly what the government has in mind.
The actual wording of the legislation and the way it is to be carried out will enable us to judge more readily whether the government is in earnest or whether it simply wants to fulfil some of its commitments.
As a matter of fact, unless we decide to implement the indicative planning we talked about during the last session, a planning which has brought prosperity to so many European countries, I think we will have very little chance to solve the serious unemployment problems and the serious economic problems of our country.
I hope that all those boards the government intends to set up will have a fair and equitable representation of the labour and farming communities. All elements of our economic life must be represented on those federal agencies.

I am of the opinion that the climate of confidence which surrounds this new government, which is reflected in the papers and the comments made by everybody, will promote the appearance of new capital in Canada and new investments in the most important segments of our economic life.
If I discussed economic problems and solutions contemplated by the government, it is mainly because in our province of Quebec unemployment is and has always been a plague as I shall try to prove it. That situation has been existing for a long time.
I have here a publication by the dominion bureau of statistics entitled "Unemployment in Canada", catalogue No. 71-503F. On page 12 of that document, you can read "Distribution of unemployment by region". From 1951 to 1955, a period when we had a Liberal government-one must admit that-36 per cent of all jobless in Canada were in the province of Quebec. From 1956 to 1960, when we had a Conservative government for most of the time, 36 per cent of jobless lived in the province of Quebec. In 1961, the proportion is still 35 per cent while we only had 27 per cent of the labour force.
It is obvious that unemployment has particular effects on personal income. I have before me a document which shows that there was $497 difference, in 1961, in the personal income as between a resident of Ontario and a resident of Quebec; this means that in
The Address-Mr. Sauve Ontario, the per capita income was $1,829 while in the province of Quebec it was only $1,382, a difference of 37 per cent.
Well, Mr. Speaker, how can the citizens of the province of Quebec, who consider themselves as full fledged citizens, who want to be considered as equal partners in Canada, be willing to accept a situation where they are at a financial disadvantage compared to the citizens of Ontario?
I believe that the measures set out in the speech from the throne will probably help to find a solution to the problem of unemployment. But what chances have these measures of being successful in the province of Quebec? I suggest that any legislation from the Ottawa government should get the approval of the Quebec people and of the provincial government. The pieces of legislation with which we shall have to deal in this house should facilitate the work already undertaken by the government of Quebec.
In the province of Quebec, we have set up a general investment corporation; we are planning to establish an iron-smelting industry and, unless the central government, which has great responsibilities in the economic field, comes and facilitates the renovation work undertaken by the Liberal government of Quebec, I am afraid that we, in Quebec, shall not be able to achieve the aims which we have set forth and, consequently, we shall continue to have grievances against the rest of Canada.
For the administration of these new laws, when we shall have to recruit civil servants, it will be important to choose employees from the province of Quebec, familiar with the Quebec mentality, who will be on friendly terms with the Quebec government, and with the officials from Quebec. Otherwise, how can we hope for the successful administration of these new laws?
Mr. Speaker, as far as the unemployment problem and the inferior income I have just referred to are concerned, even if the latter situation is, to my way of thinking, the main cause of the uneasiness which is felt, it remains nevertheless that, as a group, our situation is far from brilliant.
When we consider the situation of the French Canadians in the hundred largest corporations in Canada, we find that only two of them are managed by members of our group; there is not a single French Canadian vice president on the executive board of the C.N.R. or of the C.P.R. In fact, until recently, not a single French Canadian was a member of the executive board of the C.N.R. Why did we have to utter shrill protests in this house

The Address-Mr. Sauve before Mr. Maurice Archer was appointed? What can we infer from this?
You will note that two French Canadians have been prime ministers of Canada; that three have been chief justices of the supreme court and one, Governor General. But why are there no French Canadians to be found to manage more crown corporations as well as the large Canadian banks?
It should nevertheless be appreciated that we have been waiting since 1867. We have been patient. It is difficult to ask a people to keep on waiting, when that people has known, since the month of September 1959, a climate of freedom.
That people who want to develop is creating the instruments of its own freeing and goes on with its emancipation, as it can be seen now.
Things that seem irregular happen too often. For instance, on the trains between Montreal and Ottawa-on both the C.N.R. and the C.P.R.-conductors are practically unilingual and the announcements are called only in English. And while this happens in Ottawa and on the trains, bombs are exploding in Montreal. Even in government buildings, elevator operators do not always understand French. Most of the time, if we want to go to the fourth floor, they take us up to the sixth.
Such is the situation at the present time. It should at least be realized what a climate it creates. We have practically no right to live in French in certain provinces.
In the economic field, where do we stand? We own almost nothing. We have almost nothing, outside the province of Quebec.
As to the civil service in Ottawa, even if they say to French Canadians: "Come, you will be welcome", our civil servants must nevertheless write and discuss in English. In the important international meetings, how many French Canadian officials represent us? Indeed I intend to put this question on the order paper of the house.
There must be a possible solution to that problem. We cannot wait any longer.
The proposed enquiry on biculturalism will soon get under way, but naturally it will not solve all our problems. However, it might increase our awareness of the situation, and enlighten more particularly our English speaking friends. For most French speaking Canadians, the problem is of a psychological order. If we are not really happy outside Quebec, if the education of our children in the other provinces is fraught with difficulties,

if we must fight to snatch mere crumbs from the various provincial governments, how then can we be proud of our country and feel at home everywhere within the Canadian borders? It is high time for all of us to size up the situation.
The commission on biculturalism will only succeed if it secures the co-operation of the provinces. If this co-operation is denied, what could the commission do? We know that most of our problems stem from education, a matter strictly within the jurisdiction of provincial governments. The success of the inquiry rests also in part upon the choice of the commissioners. I hope that the provinces and the federal government will select the best men, and discard every vestige of partisanship.
I think we are all agreed on that point. The success of the inquiry on biculturalism will depend in great part on the excellence of the briefs to be submitted to the commission. If the two main racial groups of our country take advantage of this inquiry to give expression to their spite toward one another, its results will be inconclusive. Briefs must be objective.
I trust that the inquiry will have at its disposal all the means required for objective and scientific research in order to find out what is going on and what is exactly the situation at the present time. Being aware of the situation, we shall be in a better position to find the proper answers to our problems.
Let us not believe, however, that those answers will be found overnight, because even though the federal government were to accept the proposals of Mr. Lesage, the matter would not be entirely settled because it goes beyond the problem of fiscal relations.
I, for one, believe that the federal government could accept the terms of the Quebec government and propose to the other provinces the same arrangements whereby the federal government's share of expenses would be turned over to the provinces in the fields coming under provincial jurisdiction. Let me explain.
Supposing that the fiscal demands of the province of Quebec would amount to $125 million a year, the federal government might very well hand over those $125 million to the province while the province would have to pay, at the same time, the federal contribution of $75 million to hospital insurance and do the same in other fields.
What Quebec wants, is self-administration in its own way. The province does not want to take what rightly belongs to others, but it wants to be able to look after its own, affairs in all fields under its jurisdiction.

You will note, Mr. Speaker, that it we want to be our own masters at home, it does not mean that we want to separate ourselves from the others, though-and here I am weighing my words carefully-we find, more and more, in the province of Quebec, people who do not expect anything either from Ottawa or from the rest of Canada.
Those people are not necessarily separatists. But they have decided to solve their own problems themselves through a government which is nearer to them, i.e. the provincial government of Quebec.
I trust-my speaking time is about up- that all my fellow members will realize the importance of the legislation suggested by the Liberal government in Ottawa. I also hope that they will not tarry in passing economic legislation, which might end part of our troubles, because we of the province of Quebec want to live in the same way as others do. We want to live as others do, as do people in Ontario, and enjoy the same prosperity. We want to feel at home everywhere in Canada. When we get out of the province of Quebec, we want to find ourselves at home too, be it in Vancouver, Winnipeg or St. John's, Newfoundland. For this is our country, the country of all Canadians. And, which is perhaps still more important, we would like the people from the other provinces to want us too.
We want to feel that we are essential to the development of Canada. We want the rest of Canada to like us. If Canadians from all provinces will join with us, we will build in Canada, our land as well as yours, a country where it feels good to live in good understanding and complete equality. We want to be equal partners.
It is probably the last chance the traditional political parties will have in the province of Quebec. No longer can we accept promises from political parties in that field. Now, we need action. We have become politically conscious. We all know what happened last June when the people of Quebec gave a warning to all traditional parties, voting as they did for Social Credit. The province of Quebec gave that warning and they might give more than a warning at the next election, unless we, who are responsible for the government, take courageous and necessary measures. But I think those measures are forecast in the speech from the throne. I am
The Address-Mr. Paul proud to belong to a party with a leader such as the Hon. Lester B. Pearson.

Our Socred friends did not seem to relish those results; let them not worry, for I will have a few words to say about them in a minute. The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne gives us an opportunity to deal with just about every subject, provided, however, that the discussion can be constructive, for one should not forget that the present government is a minority government.
Hon. members all remember the enthusiasm shown by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson)-and I take this opportunity to congratulate him for his recent appointment to the privy council of Her Majesty the Queen-when he said the day after the election of June 18, 1962:
We must have an election.
The lust for power was the driving force behind him. It is interesting to read the comments made in this house by the then leader of the opposition on October 1, 1962. I believe that his words are still timely today. This is what we find at page 50 of official Hansard:
The first business of this parliament once the formalities have been completed. .. must be to decide in accordance with our constitutional and demo-

cratic rights whether the minority government now in office has the confidence of this House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, 41 per cent of voters voted for the Liberal party. Therefore, the government which is leading us presently does not have the confidence of the people. In fact, the Prime Minister made a statement in 1962 which can very well apply to the situation we have today. This is what he said:
In the present circumstances, such a motion takes precedence over other business-
The Prime Minister of today was speaking of a non-confidence motion.
-as it has done in the past in similar circumstances. For this purpose it is the duty and the privilege of the official opposition to move a motion which will make that decision possible. That duty is obvious. Indeed, it is inescapable, when nearly 63 per cent of the voters in this country have declared in the recent election that they have no confidence in this government, in its policies and in its leadership.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that there is nothing to be changed in this statement except that 61 per cent must be substituted for 63 per cent.
The then leader of the opposition went on to say:
Will it help Canada if, by voting confidence in this minority government, we reject this verdict of the people, ignore the records, and deny the validity of positions previously taken, and declared by those who took them to be in the national interest? There can be no stability in government when over any substantial period the party in power cannot ordinarily command the majority in the House of Commons.
It was interesting to note the concern shown last night by the hon. members opposite. As a matter of fact, they were pale, which reminded me then of the words of Louis Veuil-lot: "Let us beware of pale faces". They were all nervous, because they remembered no doubt the statement made by their leader on October 1, 1962. But the present situation is a little more complicated and confused.
Mr. Speaker, until Good Friday of this year, the Canadian people were not sure which one of the two main parties would form the next government. But then came a turncoat movement, a sort of political osmosis, the sudden joining of six Social Crediters who were drawn to the Liberal party, either to protest their own interests, or from conviction, or for a sense of security, or for money, I know not what. But the present right hon. Prime Minister had such a lust for power that, on the very day that group of six joined forces with him-later, they had to withdraw-he hastened to express his satisfaction at getting the support brought to him by six Social Credit members.

Well, if the former Conservative government has been taken to task for remaining in power with the help of the Social Credit party, then I would say to my Liberal friends, have no fear, because you were lucky last night.
We hope that the members of the Social Credit party will be true to the statement they made during the election campaign, that is, not to be the servants of another political party, but to remain true to their mandate by working first of all for the welfare of the people, as every member of this house is duty bound to do.
Mr. Speaker, we noted a great contrast between the uncalled for interventions of the present Prime Minister, when he was leader of the opposition, last June, and the calm, the seriousness with which the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) greeted the people of Canada, last April 21 and wished good luck to the new Liberal government, while assuring the people that the opposition would not systematically practice obstruction, as our hon. friends opposite did during the last parliament. That is why, last night, as a national issue was at stake, and not in order to indulge in a systematic opposition, but because we had, at this time, to take a stand on a question in accordance with the Conservative party policy, we did not fear to vote for the subamendment.
And, Mr. Speaker, it is difficult not to mention the lack of interest with which the members of the cabinet seem to listen to the speeches offering solutions to the problems , discussed since the beginning of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In fact, there is only one minister in the house this afternoon, while the members are dealing with various matters that might interest various departments. But I hope that the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis), who is at his desk right now, will let his fellow cabinet members know about the various recommendations, suggestions and criticisms that are made by the members.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the house to certain events, not unusual, but somewhat strange, that happened in my riding during the last election campaign. I want to tell you that following some calls that I made in my riding since last April 8, I found that some of my constituents felt that they had lost some of their independence.
How the Canadian people feel outside the limits of my riding, I cannot tell, but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that back home, in

That will certainly be the only time I shall agree with the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) during the present session.
Mr. Speaker, there has been a shameful patronage going on in the province of Quebec. Everything has been done to bring about the triumph of the Liberal party. There has been blackmail, individuals have been threatened with withdrawal of their welfare pensions and indigent mothers of their allowance, invalids saw their pensions threatened, and the same happened to farmers with regard to farm credit payments if the mother and father would vote or if the grown boys and girls did.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I shall with great pride render tribute to the people of Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere, who remained unmoved by such threats and promises, who have proved to be above any immediate material gains, and remained faithful to the Conservative party, not because of him who is now speaking to you, but because the Conservative party advocates, and always will advocate political independence.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) said, on January 31, 1963, in this very House of Commons, as can be seen on page 3289 of the official record:
It will, as always, honour its obligations. But it will not be pushed around or accept external domination or interference in the making of its decisions. Canada is determined to remain a firm ally, but that does not mean that she should be a satellite.

The Address-Mr. Paul
It is interesting to note developments in my riding since the Liberal gentlemen came into power. First of all, there is the matter of the Associated Textiles of Canada Limited. We can remember the distress and depression in which the textile industry had fallen when the Conservatives took over in June 1957. The employees of that industry were facing chronic unemployment; working hours had fallen to 30 or 35 a week; there was overproduction. The minister of finance and the minister of trade and commerce of the day worked together in order to improve that national production and find markets for it, and so successfully that the chairman of the manufacturing branch of the Associated Textiles of Canada Limited sent a letter to all the workers in that plant, dated December 18, 1962, in which he said:
In the year that is drawing to a close activity in the textile industry in Canada increased considerably. This is mainly due to the changes made in the value of the Canadian dollar, and to the higher tariff wall designed to protect goods manufactured in this country, which brought about a decrease of imports, while a great number of Canadian workers in the textile industry are now benefiting from this increase in production.
That was on December 18, 1962. And I hope that my hon. friends opposite will not attribute a political character to that document, as it preceded the last federal election by nearly four months. But, oddly enough, the situation is deteriorating to the point that on May 3 last, the company had to dismiss 75 employees in its textile industry at Louise-ville and the same thing is happening in St. Gabriel de Brandon and Berthierville. We have good reason to ask what new life the present government has given to the textile industry. What steps have they taken, upon assuming power, that have so paralysed that important industry of the province of Quebec.
That is not all. In my home town, Louise-ville, there is another industry, the Laminated Structures Company Limited. Every spring that company used to increase its staff and, in May, it had something like 150 to 175 employees. This year, on May 3 last, the company had to fire 29 workers. How can you explain such a situation? How is it that several labourers or tradesmen like bricklayers, plasterers, carpenters and electricians can no longer find work in Montreal, a situation which has not occurred in the past five years. That has happened in the last two or three weeks, or in the past month.

But what measures does the government intend to take to get the Canadian production and economy moving? We shall come to that in a moment.
But there is another much more serious question and that is the intolerable lot imposed on the eastern farmers in the province of Quebec and in the Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere riding by the new Liberal government. This afternoon, we heard the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), with an inexplicable candour, state that the 25 cents subsidy per 100 pounds of milk would not be paid out anymore and that this meant a saving of $6 million for the taxpayers. Let the Liberals go and explain that statement by the Minister of Agriculture in the province of Quebec where they travelled around during the last election making believe that the Liberal party would stimulate agriculture. And what about imports of American pork arriving in Montreal by truck loads and car loads to such a point that nowadays, the farmer is not getting the price he was receiving under the Conservative administration. Is that Liberal stability?
I think some measures are necessary to cope with the situation which is becoming alarming not only for labourers, but also for textile workers and farmers. I do not intend to dwell any longer on this matter of agriculture. I know that the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) will discuss the matter in a much more capable manner than I could.
Now let us take a look at the speech from the throne-which is supposed to be the corner stone of the legislation to be introduced by the government. There are some excellent measures in the speech from the throne but others are dangerous.
First of all there is the establishment of a royal commission on bilingualism and bicul-turalism. That measure is excellent. It has been a must for a very long time and I should commend the government for having understood a problem which transcends the interests of political parties because it involves the very future of confederation and the peaceful co-existence of English speaking Canadians and French speaking Canadians throughout Canada.
The former administration under the present leader of the official opposition also had an excellent idea, that of a federal-provincial conference. In my opinion, Mr. MAY 22. 1963
Speaker, we should not put that idea aside because if we want Canada to be a bilingual country, we must go to the very heart of the problem which is a problem of education. And since education is a provincial matter under the constitution, the provinces must subscribe to the principle of bilingual education right across the country if our youth is to grow up with such a mental attitude and culture, so that when they attain maturity they may continue to practice bilingualism and biculturalism which are so necessary to the greatness and prosperity of Canada and particularly to the survival of this Canadian confederation. This matter supersedes political interests, as the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve) stated a moment ago. One must not ignore all that has been accomplished in the past, because governments have always been half aware of this fact. The Liberals have adopted measures which have been satisfactory to French Canadians and so have the Conservatives with measures which have been called "mere concessions' and I am not using these words lightly when I say "mere concessions". We are not Canadian citizens who want more than others. We only want to be treated like the English speaking citizens.
And I would remind the Anglo-Saxon Canadians that the French Canadians were never vanquished on the Plains of Abraham, in Quebec city. They were just defeated. There is a difference. Yes. We kept our civil code, our courts of justice. We had, at that time, aspirations and rights that were recognized by various measures, constitutional or otherwise. But those measures were defined in and sanctioned by an act called the British North America Act, after meetings held in Charlottetown and Quebec city, in order to treat with fairness and equity those two great pioneer nations of Canada. Well, we have no right today to remain unconcerned regarding this serious problem of biculturalism and bilingualism. We must consider a situation which has become alarming and, unfortunately, can have dire consequences for the future of the Canadian confederation.
Personally, I am in favour of calling together the French Canadian states general.
I support the measure passed last week in the legislative assembly of Quebec, both by the Liberals and the National Union party, so that that meeting can enable French Canadians to become conscious of an actual situation, study steps and means to correct it, participate in the drafting of briefs to be sub-28902-5-Hi

Let us hope that it will be possible later on to call a federal-provincial conference to facilitate the solution of that problem, as I said earlier, not to give special treatment to French Canadians, but so that they may be treated as equal partners who have fought, worked and suffered for the greatness and prosperity of the whole of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join the many voices in this house that have offered their congratulations and their good wishes to you on your election to this historic chair which Speaker James Cockbum first took in the old House of Commons to open the session of 1867 about 96 years ago. I join too with many other members in congratulating the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the members of his cabinet on their appointments and wish them success in the great task which they have undertaken.
I was touched by the eloquent words of the mover (Miss Jewett) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne as she described the beautiful villages and the fertile valleys of her own Northumberland, and I wondered as I listened how I would be received in this house when I came to describe how my own constituency of Vancouver Quadra lies between 16th avenue on the one hand and 37th avenue on the other. I admired too the brief and cogent words of the seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne and I congratulate him upon setting an excellent precedent for the new members of this house to follow.
I wish to say a few words about my distinguished opponent in the past election. Few persons in Canadian public life have achieved such a reputation as the Hon. Howard Green for unswerving loyalty and integrity. He first entered the house in 1935, the same year as my late father, who entered parliament in that year as the Liberal member for North Huron. He reminded me of this on election night when the battle was over and he came to our committee rooms and told us that if he had to be defeated he preferred to be defeated by the son of a man whom he had personally known and had respected in this house. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members on this side of the house will grant me a few moments

The Address-Mr. Deachman
to salute this great Canadian, soldier and parliamentarian, who served his country for a lifetime, as few are given to serve it, in war and peace.
I deem it a high honour to follow him as the second member of parliament to be elected for Vancouver Quadra and the first to serve it as a member of the Liberal party. I return to this beautiful city of Ottawa after an absence of over 20 years during which I have seen it only fleetingly. Not much has changed. There was a May blizzard terrifying the tulips when I arrived, but the next day the sun blazed and the whole city was defrosted in a few hours. The old pavement along Rideau street is still the same and it jarred my memory and my spine. But the new government buildings, the tall apartment buildings and the burgeoning suburbs around the periphery of Ottawa reminded me that this capital has kept pace year by year with the growth of the nation.
I was astonished a little to see the new art gallery which looks like our post office in Vancouver. I remember that a distinguished visitor from this city to Vancouver told us on one occasion that we should put a slipcover over our post office. Here in Ottawa the quiet, old, stone convents, shuttered and curtained, the green patina of copper roofs and the gingerbread topping on the old east block still link us with our historic past and with the city of Laurier.
On the coast, and I know I will be understood by easterners who come from the "island" or from the "bay" if I just refer to it as the coast, we have no long history. In 1842 Henry Goulburn, British chancellor of the exchequer, said:
These territories are bounded by frost and wrapped in fog, and woe betide any unfortunate individual who might be so far diverted from the path of prudence to settle in these parts.
But by 1908 Rudyard Kipling had come by. He thought a little better of it and said:
Such a land is good for an energetic man. It is also not so bad for a loafer.
Not very long ago I met Greg Clark in Victoria and he said to me:
Anybody who can live on the coast and doesn't is an idiot.
So we are improving.
The constituency which I have the honour to serve was named after two gallant seamen, Captain Vancouver, who first mapped the inland waters of the coast and whose maps were so very good that they are still in use in parts today, and Admiral Quadra, a Spanish sailor who knew those waters in the days when the coast was claimed by Spain.
There are no great factories, office buildings, forests or farms in my constituency. It lies in the heart of residential Vancouver and

is the home of many men and women who daily earn their living in the city.
The University of British Columbia, which now enrolls 13,000 students in its degree courses and instructs almost as many more in its post-graduate and summer courses, is located in Vancouver Quadra. On a spacious promontory overlooking the sea it faces on the west towards the strait of Georgia and the waters of the Pacific, and on the north and east towards the coastal mountains, rising dramatically and abruptly from the sea to heights of 5,000 feet. We make no boast when we say there is no other university in the world more beautifully situated than this.
Millions of dollars of provincial money and private contributions are involved in the building program now under way at our university. Funds from the Canada Council have also contributed to the extension of the library, the building of dormitories and the construction of the new fine arts theatre and centre, which is now reaching completion on that campus to make it one of the finest in north America. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation loans also assist in dormitory construction, so that the federal government has a considerable role in the improvement of that university.
It is in the field of operating costs that universities find their greatest troubles. There seems to be ample desire to build buildings, provide equipment, grant scholarships and bursaries and finance research projects. But no one, provincial or federal, private or public, has any real enthusiasm for paying the operating costs. How to pay for the daily operating charges of universities is becoming an acute provincial problem and one in which the federal government must find ways to play an increasingly important part, if our universities are to expand in keeping with the expansion of the country.
A military district headquarters is located in Vancouver Quadra. The Department of National Defence keeps a faultlessly neat establishment there and its military personnel are good neighbours. But it is situated on a choice beach property which impedes the development of Vancouver's scenic Marine drive and public beaches. Proud as we are of this establishment and the fine Canadian soldiers who operate it, we residents of Vancouver look to the day, not too distant I hope, when this property can be released for the completion of the parks and drives and beaches which will make the littoral of English bay one of the finest anywhere.
I believe I sensed last night that there are more vital issues than this pressing the Minister of National Defence. But I can assure

him that there is none which he could solve more easily and which would give him more pleasure in doing it.
There is one other federal institute of size in Vancouver Quadra. Shaughnessy military hospital, with a thousand beds, is one of the great general hospitals in Canada built to serve our veterans. At one time its beds were filled with veterans undergoing treatment for service wounds and disabilities. Its patients were young. The hospital's cases were acute. The staff doctors who walked its corridors were the best of the civilian specialists in the city of Vancouver. Nowhere in Canada could a man obtain more superlative treatment and care than in Shaughnessy.
Today, circumstances have changed. Service wounds and disabilities form only a small fraction of present cases. Many beds are filled with aging veterans. They present problems of chronic care, and single patients tend to occupy beds for periods of weeks and even months. The specialists who gave Shaughnessy its enviable reputation have tended to drift away. So have many of the acute, non-service cases which formerly were treated there.
Thus, a magnificent general hospital of 1,000 beds, which would cost $20,000 to $25,000 a bed to build today, has become, for the greater part, an institute for the terminal care of the aged. We owe such care to our aging veterans, Mr. Speaker, but is it necessary that chronic care be administered in the highest priced, best equipped, most modern general hospital beds in the land?
As medicare plans are developed, the number of acute hospital cases will rise simply because people will be given the opportunity for the first time to obtain long deferred elective treatment. Existing general beds will, in all probability, not be able to accommodate the flood of new cases.

The Address-Mr. Coates so that with less than 9 per cent of the population, British Columbia accounted for more than 17 per cent of the value of Canada's export trade.

Aviation is the second largest secondary industry in the whole of British Columbia, and one of great importance to us on the coast in providing connections on short hops throughout the whole of British Columbia's indented and serrated coast.

I should like also to congratulate the hon. members on this side of the house who moved and seconded the address in reply. They are a credit to their constituencies and to this party. Everywhere in this country, women as well as men, are today voicing their pride in the performance in this house of the hon. and charming member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett).
As the member for Spadina, Mr. Speaker, the most cosmopolitan riding in Canada, I should like to say a word of tribute at the outset to the former member for Spadina, Mr. Charles Ted Rea, who has been seriously ill and has recovered to a limited extent only. I know from meeting many people in my riding and from meeting members here who knew him, particularly members on the opposite side, that he is a well liked and respected man. He was the able deputy of committees in the twenty fourth parliament, when he suffered a stroke. He made a decision against his own interests that he could not in fairness stand for re-election. On your behalf, and on my own, I wish him well.
Mr. Rea was first elected in Spadina in a by-election in 1955 after Colonel David Croll resigned his seat. Colonel Croll, of course, was elevated to the Senate. Senator Croll, as you know, is equally as active in the Senate

as he was in the house. As the Liberal senator for Spadina, he continues to bring honour to my constituency. As a speaker in demand during the last election campaign, Senator Croll's activities were the toast of this party and the scourge of the opposition. I am pleased to follow both of these fine men and I hope to emulate their good work.
My riding is one of the central ones in the city of Toronto. It is known for its infinite variety of nationality, race and creed, as well as for its extremes of wealth and poverty. Particularly since the last war the southern part has been a reception area for landed immigrants from different nations. Succeeding groups settle closely together under crowded housing conditions and then, as they adjust themselves, tend to settle throughout the metropolitan area. However, each group always seems to leave at least a small core behind, and this gives the business streets of Spadina, particularly the famous Kensington market a distinct international flavour. Symbolic of this is the widespread use of the espresso coffee percolator.
There are more than the usual number of retail and wholesale stores, the best known one being the ecstatic establishment of that prince of discounters, Honest Ed. There are many multistoried manufacturing plants in the southern industrial area of the riding, large railway yards and a new expressway. Spadina avenue itself is still the Ontario centre of the garment industry and great numbers from both within and without the riding are employed in the needle trades, usually on a piecework basis.
Although the work of making cloth, fur coats and other articles of wearing apparel is wonderfully satisfying, it is a trade that has a high, early lay-off rate as aging fingers become less and less nimble. There is some need, therefore, to plan and carry out retraining of not only the unemployed but also of those who may become so.
Spadina is bounded on the north by the south limit of Forest Hill village and on the south by the waterfront of lake Ontario. It includes Toronto island. Although the map of Spadina resembles a Christmas stocking, all within its boundaries is not always Christmasy.
The main problem is lack of sufficient steady work, both for willing immigrants and for willing Canadians from depressed areas who migrate to Toronto. For Spadina, the loans and grants of the municipal development and loan board to the city of Toronto, with the approval of the province, should prove to be a godsend. It is true that there are many existing statutes offering aid to municipalities, but they mostly require a sharing agreement between the three levels

of government and pertain to one class or object of construction, or else have a higher interest rate. The existing aids are not used as often as they might be because municipalities are unwilling to take the initiative in fields selected by the federal government. In the main, they found that if they did go ahead the construction program often created an accompanying problem. Now, under the proposed legislation municipalities will be able to pick their own projects, obtain the necessary loan or grant and proceed on their own plan. Thus, subways, clearances, redevelopments, public housing, sewers and water works projects, together with other urban and suburban service renewals should be eligible, under this proposed plan, for low interest loans.
The central part of my riding is densely populated. Many are not yet citizens. Some are political refugees who hide acute feelings but who struggle and succeed in this strange but wonderful new land. Those who acquire the language quickly are the happiest and usually the most successful. Many have brought new skills with them to Canada and have made new fortunes in a surprisingly short time.
Unless she goes to business, the wife of .an immigrant has great difficulty in learning English. She longs for her native land and occasionally becomes so homesick that she and her whole family will return; but most desire to remain to provide their children with the great opportunities that they readily see this country affords.
There are an unusual number of well attended churches and synagogues in my riding and, of course, the famous Scott mission with its sad lineups of hungry men stretching along the sidewalks of Spadina avenue. Another structure well known to the unemployed is the ancient unemployment insurance commission office on Spadina avenue, where men and women ride up and down in rickety elevators and stand in line for hours and hours. They hope, as I do, for increased benefits, less waiting and less need to be there.
Other buildings of note are Casa Loma, perched in the north end on the shore line of ancient glacial lake Iroquois, the Primrose club on St. Clair avenue west, the medical arts building on Bloor street west, the Toronto reference library on College street, the Toronto Western hospital on Bathurst street and the fine new publishing plant of the evening Telegram on Front street west, designed specifically to be heated by a new and independent principle to complement, no doubt, its new, independent policy. Well, he used his head in any event. We have some lovely high-rise apartments in the riding which are replacing many grand old homes that are now too hard to carry even as guest homes. The University of Toronto has expropriated many blocks of houses and stores west of St. George street- I know many of you know Toronto very well -torn them down and already erected several fine new university buildings.
The Toronto islands boast of the Royal Canadian and Island yacht clubs, an airport, a beautiful municipal park and many year-round homes built on lands leased from the city on Ward's, Algonquin and Centre islands.
The islands are at present reached by ferries from the foot of Bay street. These are a pleasant means of transportation in the summertime but in this day and age they are somewhat anachronistic. Certainly they are slow and costly to maintain. A tunnel or other satisfactory modern means of access to these islands is badly needed, particularly to give the working man and his family access to a delightfully restful place where they can go in their leisure time at little expense. Indeed, a former federal government had at one time planned to provide such a tunnel at its entire expense but it was prevented from doing so when it met the same fate as did the last government a few weeks ago.
Responsibility for access to these islands should again be recognized, I submit, as primarily the responsibility of the federal government because the dredging of the eastern and western channels prevents the islands from becoming naturally accessible by fill sands drifting from Scarborough bluffs. The beds of both channels lead into Toronto harbour. As most hon. members probably well know, these beds and the bed of the harbour are federal property.
Since the opening of the seaway colourful ships from all over the world enter Toronto harbour, usually by the western channel or western gap as it is more familiarly called. Lightly loaded or shallow draught vessels usually leave by the eastern gap where a dredging problem arises more frequently. Because of the great increase of traffic in the harbour a lift bridge across either of the channels would not be too feasible. I understand that the Toronto harbour commission has redrafted a plan for a tunnel from the foot of Bathurst street under the western gap to the island airport, and it is my hope that this

I would estimate that the two largest national groups in my riding are the Italian and the Hungarian. The section of College street between Bathurst and Grace is affectionately called "Little Italy" and on the side streets north and south of College many immigrants make their own "vino" as they did back home. For this purpose they import grapes from California by the carload. After visiting many of these hospitable homes one becomes impressed with the money and effort that has been put into improving their interiors and their furnishings. In many homes and backyards there are plants and gardens that are reminiscent of the walled estates of Italy, only on a smaller scale.

Spadina has since the year 1956 probably been the largest reception area in Canada for immigrating Hungarians, Serbs, Slovenians and Croatians. The freedom fighters and those who followed them have taken to their adopted land with enthusiasm and are noticeably eager to acquire citizenship. For them the most popular man in this country is the former minister of citizenship and immigration who is now the Secretary of State for Canada (Mr. Pickersgill). They are most appreciative of his efforts on their behalf when he went to Austria in 1956 to assist their entry here. In fact, if I want to raise a cheer in some audiences I find I simply have to mention the name of the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill. May I call it six o'clock?
